claims.text: In-situ high-resolution TEM heating can investigate thermally induced structural changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at the atomic scale.
The observed thermal structural changes will correlate with high-entropy stabilization.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will maintain overall phase integrity at moderate temperatures.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will display slight lattice distortion or local segregation at higher temperatures.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic and have uniform size and crystallinity.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a homogeneous atomic distribution.
Heating from room temperature to approximately 1000°C in a TEM heating holder is the proposed intervention.
Temperature steps of 50–100°C will enable transient atomic-scale changes to be captured.
Atomic diffusion and local rearrangements at defects or boundaries mediate phase integrity under thermal stress.
High configurational entropy reduces the driving force for phase separation.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a random solid solution in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Enhanced atomic mobility can produce local rearrangement or segregation that is detectable by atomic-scale imaging.
At moderate temperatures, AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will retain a uniform crystalline structure.
Near 1000°C, AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will show increased lattice disorder or localized compositional inhomogeneity.
The high-temperature structural changes will be subtler than those in conventional alloys lacking high-entropy stabilization.
Room-temperature AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have uniform crystallinity, homogeneous elemental distribution, and no detectable phase separation.
Imaging resolution, oxidation, and beam-induced effects can limit in-situ TEM observations at very high temperatures.
The onset temperature and extent of atomic rearrangement in high-entropy nanoparticles are uncertain because empirical data are limited.
